en: Preface to the Recorded Sayings of Master Fangshan:
Now, among those rare treasures hidden away by those who have transcended the world, none surpasses the pearl of Emperor Yang or the jade of Bian He;
these are the ultimate examples. In the autumn of the Ren-shen year, I passed through Zhulin (Zuili) and visited my elder brother Huaiyue at Li Village in Changtang.
While sitting in the study hall amidst a tea gathering, he presented me with the *Record of Master Fangshan*. As I unfolded and read it, I struck the desk and sighed, saying:
"Is this not truly a treasure of the world? If one were to compare it to pearls and jade, those are merely common objects of the mundane realm.
This *Record of Master Fangshan* is, in truth, the true lamp that benefits the world, illuminating the dark alleys of existence; how much more so its words!"

Regarding the phrase "seeing the truth" (jianti), every single character transcends the school's tenets. Furthermore, when my elder brother Cè was traveling from our Tiantai [Mountain], he obtained this [text] from beneath the seat of an ancient Buddha statue in a ruined temple;
it was truly marvelous. When my brother first traveled to the Tai and Yan mountains, he happened upon it among discarded books beneath the pedestal of an old Buddha image in a dilapidated temple.
Amidst the decayed and moth-eaten remains, the meaning of the characters was brilliantly clear and dazzling to the eye. Upon reading the sentences closely, [I found them to be profound].
It was a rare manuscript. Upon re-examining it, I discovered it was the record of Master Bao. I immediately ordered it to be transcribed by hand;

however, I regret that its pages were so decayed and rotten that they could not withstand touch. With the beginning and end missing, only one-tenth or one-twentieth remained, which is truly a great pity.
I placed it in a chest, and it has been there for over ten years now. My brothers Cè and Huì are both natives of this village. (Kāngxī...)

In the spring of the Xinwei year, I visited my elder brother Huì at Longyuan. We stayed together for over a month, inquiring about the ancestral origins and the successive records of kōan dialogues from past generations.

He then brought out the *Record of Master Bǎo* and showed it to me, saying, "This is a treasure of your own house. My brother was filled with joy and surprise; he held the incense burner and recited it with devotion.

How could this be anything less than the appearance in the world of the glowing pearl and the Bì jade? Indeed, the glowing pearl and the Bì jade— (Note: The provided text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the full extent of the supplied passage.)
It is a rare treasure of this world. Yet the Dharma words of my ancestors are truly the supreme great jewels that transcend the world.

My elder brother Hei informed me, saying: "Now our Dharma-uncle Miaoyun wishes to contribute the funds from his robes and alms bowl to commission a woodblock edition, so as to ensure its wide circulation.
I beg for a word to commemorate the extraordinary fortune through which these records of our ancestors' teachings were obtained."
This is so that those who read this record in the future may understand that my elder brother Mengfan, while wandering among mountains and waters,
encountered the words and phrases of ancient sages; he refused to let them pass by lightly, but instead brought them back to me,

thereby providing instruction for those who categorize teachings into rigid divisions and those who seek to dominate others through force, regarding the true intent behind the efforts of our predecessors.
"It is self-deception. I replied, "Indeed; truly so are these words. Though I am not quick-witted, the principle [of the matter] leaves me no choice but to decline.
At dusk, I returned to my guest-window at Fan-shou, lit a lamp, and strove to compose this; it is not easy to set down in writing.
I shall submit it for inspection to the Ancient Buddha of Ruiyan, Zu Fangshan Huaiji, whose wisdom and light distinguish between what is acceptable and what is not."
Written and inscribed by Zhì'ān, a person who abandoned the world at the third generation of Biànshān on Mount Nányuè,
in prostration; the *Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Fāngshān Wénbǎo of Ruìyán Jìngtǔ Chán Monastery in Tàizhōu Prefecture*.
Compiled by Ji Yun, the sixteenth-generation descendant of the Great Stone Mountain (Dàshíshān) in Chu and Huang, who has previously beheld the ancestral lamp;
edited by Zhen Xiong, the fifteenth-generation descendant of Guqí Dàbēi Temple. Recorded by the dharma-heirs of the successor lineage. Printed by [name].
Regarding the chamber: those who ascend the hall of the Master [Confucius] hear his Way; those who ascend the hall of the Old Lord [Laozi] observe his preferences;
those who enter the room of a mountain monk seek only his bowl. With his staff, he struck the table three times in succession.

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The sentiments of the various sages exist within them, yet the net of views is difficult to penetrate. No stages are established; there is no gate for entering.

The wisdom of *prajñā* is ever-luminous, and the essence of *tathatā* is uniquely revealed. Yet scholars from all quarters have minds that lack clarity; this is entirely due to the admixture of teachings by false teachers.
Like silkworms spinning cocoons, or like snakes clinging to their burrows, they claim to have reached home and refuse to meet others."

There are some who possess intelligence, yet they use their conscious intellect to speculate, treating *tathatā* (Suchness) as a mere abstraction and mistaking *buddhadhātu* (Buddha-nature) for something vague and indistinct; how truly pitiable they are!
Upon ascending the hall at the commencement of the retreat, he fanned a fierce flame within the great chiliocosm, whereupon a single cloud suddenly billowed forth, and he raised his tongs.
In the wondrous and subtle arena, within it, iron is transmuted into gold. On the red sand dunes, amidst the Forest of Staffs (Zhālín Shān), everyone eats arsenic and drinks lethal poison;

they walk upon jagged ice and tread upon the edge of a sword. As the saying goes: "In the cauldron of boiling water, there is no place that is not hot. You all cling firmly to withered paulownia wood and guard dead ashes; when will the beans finally burst? West Hermitage now— *(Note: This passage is a Zen kōan-style discourse.

It describes the intense, perilous, and transformative nature of the Zen path, where practitioners undergo extreme trials—consuming poison, walking on ice and blades—to realize the truth. The "beans" refer to the seeds of enlightenment or the potential for awakening within the practitioner.)*
[The Master] said, "I have added charcoal to your brazier; keep it well-heated.
He then ascended the hall and let out a thunderous shout, saying, "This is the primary truth (*paramārtha-satya*). In the snap of a finger, kalpas of dust are instantly emptied."
Without crossing the ferry or the bridge, one enters directly into the treasure-store. How extraordinary! Yet he fell under the mallet of Master Gutian.

Is there anyone among the assembly who can discern this? (The question and answer are not recorded. He then cited the following: Linji addressed the assembly, saying: "Sometimes I take away the person but do not take away the environment;
sometimes I take away the environment but do not take away the person; sometimes both person and environment are taken away; sometimes neither person nor environment is taken away."
"The objects are not taken away by both. The Master said, "They are taken away. "The mountains are green and the waters are clear; the white peaches and red apricots are not taken away.
"The mountains are green and the waters are clear; the white peaches and red apricots—tell me, how is it when they are taken away? How is it when they are not taken away? After a long silence...
He gave a shout and said: "In a single stroke, he has pulled out the sword of the settled mind;
as before, it rests across his eyebrows and eyes. On the Winter Solstice, he ascended the hall and said: "The vastness of the two polarities can be measured by the astronomical chart.
The movement of the three luminaries can be gauged by the *gui* and *biao* instruments. The sound of thunder can be transmitted by bells and drums. The transformations of wind and rain can be..."
The musical tones are in harmony. Now, that which possesses form can be observed; it cannot conceal its measure. That which possesses light can be seen; it cannot hide its traces.
That which possesses sound can be heard; it cannot bury its resonance. That which possesses color can be examined; it cannot extinguish its nature.

Thus, although the principles of heaven and earth, yin and yang, are difficult to clarify, they may still be measured through technical calculations (*shushu*); yet the nature of human beings and things—

The subtlety of the fundamental nature cannot be fathomed by the conscious mind. This is why a thousand sages have arisen one after another and ten thousand worthies have followed in succession, speaking crosswise and lengthwise, speaking upside down and sideways, and speaking of the "Vajra Ring" and the "Thorny Jujube"—speaking in all these various ways, they desire only that people [realize it].

Accept it directly and immediately. Today, West Hermitage will vomit forth his five viscera and six bowels all at once, so that everyone may recognize what is within the belly of this Elder West Hermitage.

Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "In the practice of Chan, it is not the enlightenment of the mind that is prized; in the recitation of sutras, how could it be for the sake of attaining principles?
Bian He wept while clutching his jade, grieving that the carving and polishing were fruitless; Mozi grasped his silk and lamented, sighing over how complications arise of their own accord.
To forget achievement and sever all assertions is what is prized: that there be a path for one’s emergence."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Ants have no speech, yet they can manage affairs; flies have no discernment, yet they can distinguish odors.
'Buddha' means awakening; 'Dharma' means phrases. As for the iron hammer without holes and the felt clappers—would you be willing to become a Buddha through these?"
Ascending the hall, he said: "Dharma’s wall-gazing was not because he did not understand the language of Tang. Lu Zu’s wall-gazing—what was it that he did not understand?
If you can realize this here, you will grasp the message before the first signs have even manifested; you will hold the standard and scale already commanded by the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
It will reach the point where empty space opens in solemnity and the great earth looks up in reliance. As for the solitary Lazy Old Man Zan, he was simply one-legged."
With one misstep, he retreated to the summit of Mount Sāla. "Brother Hanshan! Brother Shide! they called out to one another as they stepped upon the stone bridge.
Once they had left the mountain, they never returned. Why? Because it was thought that a red-bearded man existed, yet there was yet another with a red beard and a red chin.
Ascending the hall: At the assembly on Vulture Peak, the grass was a fathom deep; before the peak of Shaoshi, the snow was three feet deep.
Plucking the strings while the pegs remain fixed, only two are permitted.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Broad-forehead casts his sword; there is not even ground for planting a needle. The Dragon Girl offers her pearl; she still has much to look back upon.
Within the gate of the patch-robed monks, one is uniquely liberated and without dependence. Not a thread of silk hangs—how so?"
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Throughout the Great Tang Empire, everyone is but a fellow eating dregs of wine.
Here at Ruiyan, I want someone who does not understand Chan to serve as National Teacher—where could such a person be found?"
Ascending the hall: "Once the Three Barriers have been penetrated, why must one steal the tally? To deploy an extraordinary force, one must first examine the official seal.
Ascending the hall, Baiyun said: "If you truly manage to break out a sweat once, a jade palace and crystal halls will manifest upon a single blade of grass.
If you truly do not break out a sweat once, the jade palace and crystal halls will be obscured by that single blade of grass. White.
Master Yun said: "As he has thus reported, it seems the moon of the heavens has been hidden away, yet the stars of the Han lands still remain.
Ruiyan, however, was not like this; he truly managed to break into a sweat once. When the ravines were filled and the valleys were blocked, he truly could not break into a sweat once;
with his bundle tied and his hat on his head, wandering by morning and staying by evening, he was nonetheless content and joyful within himself. Why was this so?
He did not see the Way. "Auspicious grass grows in the courtyard; better that such good things never happened.

Ascending the hall, he cited Dongshan’s address to the assembly: "At the end of summer and the beginning of autumn, brothers, whether you go east or west, you must head toward a place ten thousand miles away where there is not a single blade of grass.
But as for that place ten thousand miles away where there is not a single blade of grass—how does one go there?"
Later, a monk recounted this to Shishuang. Shishuang said, “Stepping out the door, it is all weeds.
Dongshan said, “In the Great Tang Empire, how many people could there be [who understand this]? National Teacher Guoqing said, “One person has a ten-character barrier upon their tongue;
another has five-colored threads beneath their feet. If you can examine and identify these, I will give you a pair of straw sandals. The Master said, “These two venerable ones...”
Last night, one man wore three mountains upon his head; another trod upon the four seas. They met, yet did not recognize one another.
When the Old Man of Guoqing speaks thus, is it a word of praise or a word of reproach? The fundamental root has not yet been brought forth.

Setting aside for a moment the place where there is not a single blade of grass ten thousand miles away, consider this: when Shishuang said, "Once you step out the door, it is all grass," what was his intention? Can you discern it?
[He] came forth. "I give you two taels of white silver.

He ascended the hall and raised the following case: A monk asked Yunmen, "At the end of autumn and the beginning of summer, if someone suddenly asks you on the road ahead, with what will you respond?"
Yunmen said, "The assembly, step back. He asked, "Where does the fault lie? Yunmen said, "Bring me back the payment for ninety days' worth of rice.
National Teacher Qing said, "To enter a tiger's den and seek its cub is no easy task; yet this monk, alas, is dead upon level ground.
"Assembly, do you wish to recognize Yunmen? One foot is short, one foot is long. The Master said, "Knock!"
Drawing marrow from empty space; carving out sutra scrolls from a speck of dust. This is the natural livelihood of the patch-robed monk.
This monk has entered the Dragon Gate, yet he is unacquainted with the currents of the water. It is precisely because he is so overly clear that his attainment is delayed.
The assembly, do you wish to recognize Yunmen? Try looking at what Guoqing says.
Ascending the hall, he said: "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing. It stands out so abruptly that it is difficult to discern.
It cannot be named, it cannot be described, it cannot be categorized—it makes the onlookers laugh to death. O Great Assembly! Old man Ruiyan is going to let you all be free and easy.
He threw down his whisk and said: "The green mountains only know how to grind through ages; the flowing water has never..."
Washing Away Right and Wrong.

Entering the Hall, he raised the case of National Teacher Qing, who said: "Within the shadows of the Five Peaks, amidst the sounds of the Twin Streams, there is a great treasure trove, radiant on all eight sides.
Everyone here has spent so much time reaching for it; why then cannot you see it with your own eyes?"
"It is simply said to be unpassable. Today, I, this mountain monk, shall open it up directly.
[He raises his staff and says: This is Mipamā’s single-pronged fork. [He holds the staff horizontally and says:
This is Daowu’s single-edged sword. [He draws three circles and says: These are Xuefeng’s three wooden balls. A-he-he! It is not Caoxi."
On the road, atop a banner pole, the wind moves and the banner moves; from south to north, from west to east. The Master said:
"The hundreds of thousands of samādhis and immeasurable dharma-gates—if explained as a single phrase, the Buddhas and Patriarchs would swallow their voices;
if not explained as a single phrase, it would burden the thousand sages. To say 'neither of these' is yet another way of speaking without speaking. Now, let us speak."
"What more need be said? It would be better to report the truth to the great assembly and achieve a state of liberation.
He suddenly took up his staff and said, "This is the staff of Ruiyan. What do you call the 'Bimoxa Fork'? What do you call the 'Sword of Daowu'?
Furthermore, what do you call the 'Snow Peak Ball'? The old man of Guoqing speaks thus; after all, is it the wind that moves, or the banner? The banner...
"Stirring the wind. Shuigan (Ruiyan) ate his mother’s birthright until he reached this very point.
Everyone, take care! He ascended the hall and said, citing Guishan: "A high-ranking traveler must sit amidst sounds and forms, and lie down amidst sounds and forms.
Shushan came forward and asked, "What is the phrase that does not fall into sounds and forms? Guishan held up his whisk. Shushan said: [The Master] "..."
This was still merely falling into the trap of words regarding sound and form. Mian returned to his quarters; since Shanshan did not find resonance there, he took his leave of Xiangyan.
Xiangyan said, "Why do you not stay for a while? He replied, "I have no affinity with the Master. Xiangyan asked, "What is it about that you do not find resonance with?"
Shan recounted the previous conversation. Yan said, "I have a saying. [Shan] asked, "What do you say? [Yan] replied, "Speech issues forth, yet it is not sound;
form appears before one, yet it is not an object. Shan said, "So there is someone here after all. Elder brother, where is your dwelling place after you leave?"
"Let me come back to keep you company. Later that evening, Guishan asked Yanguan, "Is the Dwarf Acarya still here? He replied, "He has already left.
Guishan asked, "What did you say to him? He replied, "I also spoke to him. Guishan said, "Try reciting it for me."
Yun said, "Speech issues from what is not sound; form precedes what is not a thing. Mian asked, "What did he say? Yun replied, "He deeply approved of it.
Mian burst out laughing and said, "I thought this short fellow had some merit, but it turns out he is merely stuck right here. This boy!"
"Behind there is a dwelling place; near the mountain, there is no wood to burn; near the water, there is no water to drink. The Master said:
"Miaoyan occupies the tiger's head, knowing only what is behind; Xiangyan grasps the tiger's tail, knowing only what is before. Viewed with the correct eye," [it is otherwise].
"Both of you venerable elders failed to escape the 'Heavenly Net' of Master Ai.
If you do not believe me, there will be someone to testify to this thirty years hence."
A Quanzhen Daoist is invited to ascend the hall: A thousand-pound stone roller floats upon the water; two-ounce gourd sinks to the bottom.
Fire burns the dog’s tail and the pig’s head is charred; the Southern Dipper flees into the Northern Dipper.
You all—should you possess a pair of eyes here, not only will your original life-spirit have a place of rest, but within the four modes of deportment...
In every instance, there is a path for one’s own emergence.
Entering the hall: the broken sand-pot cannot be addressed; the flower-basket cannot be gathered up.
Suddenly encountering a situation where strategy fails, he steps forward and overturns the ritual vessels, bringing about universal peace together with the Great Brahmā King.
He muttered to himself, "Although you all have mats upon which to sit, you must also skillfully protect and mind the various Bodhisattvas.
Upon hearing this, the Mountain Monk suddenly struck him with a blow to the head. The Heavenly King said, "How excellent! What a fine staff!
It would not be easy for us to take it up. Although such was his understanding, he was still slightly inferior.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "The green peach cherishes the spring breeze; the yellow chrysanthemum rejoices in the autumn rain.
Suddenly seizing his staff, he said: "This here does not involve spring or autumn. It is as lively as a dragon, as majestic as a tiger. He struck the ground once with the staff and said:

"In this place there is also the provisional, there is also the real; there is also the illuminating, and there is also the functional. How do you all deliberate upon this? At that time, a monk stepped forward.
"Hai! The Master struck him, saying, "Are you not afraid that bystanders will laugh? The monk hesitated, and the Master struck him again.

On the occasion of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, he ascended the hall and said: "As the sūtra states: 'There is not the slightest dharma entered by wisdom, nor is there the slightest wisdom that enters into dharmas.
Therefore, one sets up a single arrow of wisdom to destroy the armies of Māra, and brandishes a single blade of prajñā."
To sever the net of all doubts is the power of wondrous awakening. If this were not yet the case, then even if one cultivates wisdom, one would not enter the perfect and eternal;
and even if one practices the gates of conduct, it would only increase one's arrogance. This is because one has not yet reached the gate of the single limit;

such is called the Dharma of Perfect Enlightenment, yet it is also called the Banner of Arrogance. If one truly awakens to the wondrous essence and suddenly accords with the One Vehicle, one must necessarily [cultivate] merit...
When both wisdom and skillful means are perfected, and both practice and understanding have reached their consummation, one takes a single step and directly treads upon the crown of Vairocana’s head;

with a single snap of the fingers, one travels throughout billions of lands. Manifesting various clouds of Bodhisattva bodies, one accomplishes the infinite and boundless sublime deeds throughout all Buddha-worlds.
If one can achieve this, then every lifting and lowering of the feet is none other than the City of Blessings; whether entering the forest or emerging from it, [one is always there].
The forest is entirely the wondrous peak; relying upon the great ocean of Mañjuśrī’s wisdom, the lion roars.

Entering into the pores of Samantabhadra, the elephant king looks back. Opening the pavilions of Maitreya, every dharma and every instance is never abandoned, manifesting the compassionate countenance of Avalokiteśvara.
Where dust mote meets dust mote and world-system meets world-system, they shine in mutual radiance. If one is not such a person, look instead to Sudhana.
For those who have first come to study, why did the Bhikṣu Dechen meet him on a distant peak?
If you can see through this here, I will guarantee for you that this matter shall never be in vain.
Small Assembly Sermon. To practice Chan and study the Way is the foremost great matter for transcending the world.

To resolve and be liberated from birth and death, one must possess the eye that discerns dharmas, distinguishing the heterodox from the orthodox and recognizing the good from the bad. In choosing friends, one must be principled, so that you may mutually encourage and inspire one another.
Formerly, when Master Nan was under the assembly at Letan, Yunfeng saw him once and called him a vessel for the Way; yet he regretted that Nan had not yet received the hammering of the true style.
One day, they went together to visit Mount Xi. At night, they discussed the Dharma-way of Yunmen.
Xuefeng said, "Although Letan is a successor of Yunmen, his Dharma-way is different. Nanping asked him why it was different. Xuefeng replied, "Yunmen is like nine-refined cinnabar;
it can transform iron into gold. Letan is like quicksilver; it may be admired for its luster, but when placed in the furnace,"
[The monk] flowed away. Nanru struck him with his pillow. The next day, Yunfeng apologized for his transgression.
Nanru said again, "Yunmen’s bearing was like that of a king; could he have been content to die under [my] words? Letan has a method for teaching people, but it is dead language.
How can dead language enliven a person? He then turned his back and left. Master Nanru called after him, saying, "If it is as you say, then who can satisfy your mind? Yunfeng—
He said, "Shishuang Yuan’s skillful means surpass those of all other quarters; you should go see him, for you must not delay.

When Master Nan went to see Shishuang, he indeed attained realization beneath the master's words. Had Master Nan not encountered Yunfeng, it would have been due to a deficiency in Yunfeng’s discernment and capacity;
otherwise, how could Master Nan’s own practice have been such? Furthermore, when Jiaoshan was presiding over the assembly, a monk asked him as follows:
"What is the Dharma-body? He replied, "The Dharma-body is without marks. "What is the Dharma-eye? He replied, "The Dharma-eye is without flaw.
At that moment, I was standing by his side and could not help but laugh. As Guishan descended from his seat, he asked me the reason for my laughter.

I said, "Venerable Master, you are one who has emerged from the crowd, yet you still have no teacher. Guishan was immediately struck with confusion and self-doubt, wishing I would explain it further for him. I—
He then pointed toward Chan Master Chuanzi. Indeed, it was through Chuanzi that he attained great enlightenment.
Had I not possessed such eyes, how could Jia Shan have come to possess them? This old man’s power of faith was insufficient and his Dharma-eye was not upright;

even though he encountered a worthy friend, he missed the mark face-to-face. Furthermore, the ways in which masters extend their hands to receive others are each different, like standing on the brink...
Jishi De Shan used the staff; one man employed the shout. Shigong set up his arrow; Luzu faced the wall. Heshan beat the drum;
Xuefeng played with a snake. Although their modes of practice differ, when they arrive home, they are one and the same.
You all, having gathered here to discern the Way and resolve the matter of birth and death, must first of all be sharp-witted and possess the proper capacity.

It must be vast and grand; it cannot be base or small. Long ago, while I was casually reading the *Platform Sutra*, I saw that when Xuánjué arrived at Caoxi, he circumambulated the Patriarch three times, struck his monk’s staff once, and stood there resolutely.
The Patriarch said, "A śramaṇa is one who possesses the three thousand dignified demeanors and eighty thousand subtle practices.
From what direction have you come, Great Virtue, that you give rise to such great arrogance? He replied, "Birth and death..."

"Affairs are great, impermanent, and swift. The Patriarch said, "Why do you not realize non-arising? To understand non-arising is to understand that there is no swiftness. He replied, "Realization itself is non-arising;
fundamentally, there is no swiftness. The Patriarch said, "So it is, so it is. Only when awakened does one possess dignified deportment.

He then prostrated and took his leave. The Patriarch said, "Is your return too swift? He replied, "Since I am fundamentally unmoving, how could there be swiftness? The Patriarch asked, "Who [is it that asks]?"

[The monk] said, "I know it is not movement. The Master said, "It is you, O benevolent one, who give rise to discrimination. The monk said, "You have deeply grasped the meaning of non-arising. The Master said, "If there is no arising, how can there be 'meaning'?
The monk said, "If there is no meaning, who would engage in discrimination? The Master said, "If there is no one to engage in discrimination, then who is it that discriminates?

At this, the mountain monk felt a joy that permeated his entire being, as if he had recovered a long-lost possession; overcome with exultation, he then related the story of the robe and bowl at Huangmei and questioned Gong.
The Zen Master said, "Since you do not understand the Buddha-dharma, why did you succeed to the Patriarchal seat? Gong said, "Not only the Patriarchs;
there are many who do not understand the Buddha-dharma yet still succeed to the Patriarchal seat. When I first entered that Way, Old Gong came down into the mud and the water to guide me.
He may truly be said to have offered his very heart, piece by piece. I simply did not recognize it."
"Like missing someone face-to-face because of likes and dislikes," he said. Therefore, he asked again, "Does the Master still succeed to the ancestral seat?
Old Gong replied, "If one succeeds to the ancestral seat, then one understands the Buddha-dharma.

At that time, although he did not understand Old Gong's meaning, fortunately he possessed the power of faith and gave rise to a great state of doubt, feeling a necessity to seek a clear understanding. He immediately requested ordination and went with his brother Ri of Tianjie.
I formed a group to visit several spiritual friends; although it yielded no immediate benefit, it was truly due to the power of being struck from the east and beaten from the west.
While at Yuyang, a monk brought the recorded words of Foguan’s ascent to the hall; upon seeing them, I immediately recognized him as a practitioner of genuine substance.
Day and night, he thought of nothing but going to see him. One day, he suddenly heard that an imperial decree had been issued, summoning him to reside at Mount Jing.

His heart was filled with joy. Within a few months, he indeed took up his staff and settled at Mount Jing. At that time, he lived in close dependence upon his elder brother, Dayi, for a very long period.

He thoroughly mastered every public case (*gong'an*) of the Buddhas and patriarchs; yet, there was only one thing he could not understand: the karmic causes arising from the four quarters and eight directions.
He repeatedly requested instruction, but [Fojian] ultimately would not speak for him. Instead, he instructed him to turn back and look within himself. Unexpectedly, Fojian fell ill.
The mountain monk, together with the assembly, requested that Fojian leave behind a verse of farewell. Fojian then took up his brush and, looking toward the mountain monk, wrote this verse:
Coming, it is empty and desolate; going, one is bare and naked. If you wish to inquire further into the ultimate point, there is the Stone Bridge at Tiantai.
Having received this instruction, I went to visit Master Duangqiao at Guoqing Temple. Whenever I entered his room to respond to his prompts, he remained entirely without obstruction.
The Master would simply smile and say nothing. I pressed him relentlessly; whenever I entered the room to seek his guidance, I did so with such urgency.
I have repeatedly received blows from the staff. One day, feeling extremely bewildered and distressed, I sat upright in my quarters.

Suddenly, seeing a fellow monk in the same hall holding a paper candle and about to enter the door, everything before me opened up with clarity. All that I had cherished throughout my life vanished in an instant.
My body and mind suddenly felt like lapis lazuli; the mountains, rivers, and the great earth were likewise like lapis lazuli, luminous both within and without.
There was not the slightest obstruction; only then did I realize that at the point where the Master extended his hand, my heels deserved twenty blows of the staff.
The next morning, I entered the abbot’s quarters to report what I had attained. The Master presented several koans in one breath to test me, and I answered each one.
He then raised the koan “All phenomena return to the One,” and I answered that as well. The Old Master—
The Master simply would not consent. He called [Shansheng] to come forward again and, making a gesture of hacking with his hand, said, "Attendant, you still owe me one stroke.
Shansheng walked out in a fit of indignation, crying out loudly, "The Master simply will not consent!

After the midday meal, during the communal work of selecting vegetables, the Master arrived shortly after; seeing that Shansheng’s hands were too weary even to move, he remarked, "The Master simply will not consent."

He suddenly asked, "Have you selected the clean ones? He replied, "They are perfectly clean. The Master reached out his hand, picked up a single root of amaranth from the basket, and threw it before the mountain monk, saying, "What is this? At that moment, the mountain monk was suddenly liberated and free from all obstruction.
The Master struck the drum and ascended the hall, addressing the assembly: "Attendant Bao has attained thorough realization. He then moved him [to a higher position].
He entered the Head Seat’s quarters alone. From that point on, he no longer doubted the Buddhas, nor the Patriarchs;
he had no doubts regarding the tenets of the Five Houses or the seventeen hundred koans. Having reached such a state, he finally became a man of no affairs.
Wandering freely between heaven and earth—this is true leisure, this is true joy. Within both the mundane and supramundane realms, there is nothing that can compare to it.
You who have cultivated a sincere heart to study the Way must reach such a state before you may find rest.
If you do not reach such a state, you must strictly avoid stopping at the illusory city along the way. As you apply yourselves to practice, arise...
Regarding the state of doubt (*yiqing*): it is not improper to take confidence in the words and phrases of the ancients; what is prized is that there be no divergence from them.

It simply lies in upholding the *huatou* (critical phrase), and one must not look upon it as a dead word. For example, when Zhaozhou saw a monk arrive for an interview, he asked: "Has the Venerable ever been to this place before?"

A monk asked, "Have you been here before? Zhaozhou said, "Go drink tea. Another monk came for an interview; Zhaozhou asked, "Have you been here before? He replied, "No, I have not. Zhaozhou said, "Go drink tea.
The head of the monastery remarked, "The Master says 'go drink tea' whether one has been here before or has not been here before.
Zhaozhou called out, "Head of the Monastery! When the head responded, Zhaozhou said, "Go drink tea. This—
These are all "live phrases. Furthermore, there was a monk who asked about the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West.
Mazu said, "The cypress tree in the courtyard. The monk said, "Master, do not point to external objects to show people. Mazu said, "I am not pointing to external objects to show people.
[The monk] asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Mazu said, "The cypress tree in the courtyard. This, too, is a live phrase. You all must believe this.
My words are simply this: apply your mind in this way; look closely and steadily; reflect back upon yourself at all times; and maintain awareness at every moment.
If the "head-word" appears before you, then press yourself into it with your whole being. If it does not appear, raise it up again and again and ask: "What is this principle?
When you say, "I do not understand," then right within that state of not understanding, let one thought endure for ten thousand years, and ten thousand years as one thought.

Reflect: seek a clear understanding of this; until you reach the ground of the ancients, do not vow to rest. Now, humans are born within heaven and earth; all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent.
Every movement and every action is a law of arising and ceasing. If one lacks the practice of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), [one cannot escape].
Yet, even if one develops an intellectual understanding of the wondrous principles of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, it will ultimately be difficult to achieve a spiritual resonance with them.
When the ancients heard of such matters, they seized the rope-head and planted their feet firmly. Some examined the state before the birth of their parents;
some examined the "Cheongju monk’s robe"; some examined "all dharmas return to One"; or some examined the koan of "three pounds of flax. They were like great generals holding their seals of command.
Ascending the dais, one takes up the reins and releases the arrow; life and death follow as appropriate. Life and death occur in an instant.

To sweep away the *chāngqiāng* (comets/obstacles) and sit in the enjoyment of great peace—if you practitioners can truly do this, piercing through mountains of silver and walls of iron, and turning your body around to look back—then not only will you grasp the news of before your parents were born, but even the cypress tree in the courtyard...
The "tree seed," the "Qingzhou cloth shirt," the "three catties of hemp," the "dry dung pellet," and the essential purport of the Five Houses—all these are within one's own house.

When it comes to uttering a single word or emitting a single phrase, they are no different from the ancients. Whether laughing, weeping, rejoicing, or reviling, everything is nothing other than the ultimate principle of Prajñā.
Therefore, the Original Teacher of Central India, out of compassion for sentient beings, arose with mercy toward the burning house.

Within, he lowered his hands to preach the Dharma for forty-nine years, expounding the sutras in over three hundred assemblies. He exhausted every nuance of the "old woman’s heart," and at the end, he held up a flower;
this was transmitted from one to another until it has shone brilliantly to this day. You, sir, are a descendant whose progeny are like a thousand waves and ten thousand billows.
One wave broadens as another rises; one surge is higher than the next. One cannot fathom its limits or shores. The ancients pierced it upon their feet and pierced it upon their hands;
they pierced it wherever they encountered a throat. They struck it on the ground; they struck it within the very nest. When they raised a shout, they struck the blue sky.
Such fellows are thought to have their hands and eyes throughout their entire bodies. Yet, were they to encounter a person of clear vision, they would find themselves at a loss.

He let out a laugh. "Why is that? he asked. "It is because one must take the ordinary household furnishings of the ancestors and present them directly before one's face, so that they are like the sky universally covering all and the earth universally supporting all, until even empty space is forced to seal its mouth and Mount Sumeru is made to tie its tongue. Even this, however, is still a 'turning phrase' (*zhuǎnjù*)."
This is not yet the ultimate standard for a monk. If we discuss this matter, it is like wrestling atop a cliff ten thousand fathoms high:
let go of your hands and go straight to the very bottom. [The Master] suddenly picks up his staff and says, "Ruigan, let go of your hands; have you ever reached the bottom yet?

He throws down the staff and says, "When one's vision is clear and sharp, one is fit to carry on the lineage; when one penetrates the wondrous principle, it is essential that it be profound and mysterious."
Small Assembly Sermon: The ancients sometimes established [the teaching], sometimes swept it away; sometimes they established within sweeping away, and sometimes they swept away within establishing.
Do you all understand this message? If you do, come forward from the assembly and speak of the principle.
Otherwise, you must recognize the Patriarch at the tips of the hundred grasses and identify him amidst the red dust.
"Son of Heaven, moreover, within this very place there is an ultimate realm; how could it be fathomed by ordinary sentiments? An ancient said:
'In this matter, to raise one's eyebrows is already to miss it; to deliberate or reflect is ten thousand miles of white clouds. Therefore it is said: 'Before one's eyes, there is no dharma.'"
The meaning lies before one’s eyes, yet it is not the dharma of the present moment; it is not something reached by the ears or the eyes.

If this matter is not attained with true depth and one’s vision is not precise, it is impossible to achieve the "clapping of hands" of Youmeng. Only when the numinous faculty is uniquely liberated can it be realized.
When the Great Function manifests, no fixed rules are maintained; the authentic command is fully presented, directly pointing to the person. How could there be any room for settling or adjusting?
If you wish to turn heaven and overturn earth, penetrating from antiquity to the present, you must stand like a ten-thousand-fathom cliff and seize the end of the rope.
Overturning all traces of obscuration, it arises in an instant. Here, those who practice silent illumination find no place to settle;
those who pursue delusions find no door to enter. If one can truly do this, everything is resolved at once and all is right;
not even a speck of dust remains. Hungry, you eat; thirsty, you drink. By day you rise; by night you sleep. Suddenly, in a moment of nonchalance, there is vast openness.

At that moment, I became clearly enlightened and finally realized that the ancients truly did not deceive me. Although one may attain such a state as this, it is precisely necessary to encounter the right person;
if one does not encounter such a person, one can do no more than lean against the gate or dwell by the door.

Thus, for a *kūn* fish spanning several thousand *li* to transform into a *péng* bird of ninety thousand *li*, one must rely on the wind from the Southern Ocean. If one places a cup in a puddle of water collected in a depression, [it will surely tip over].
Is this not as far apart as heaven and earth? Yet, while the monk’s spirit may be exhausted, his nostrils remain uplifted.
If you attempt to understand through seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing, you will be worlds away from the Way; you must reach it personally and realize it for yourself.
To merely rely on the mind of intellectual understanding is like the sun being obscured by a single cloud on some future day—do not say I did not warn you.

Small Assembly Sermon. Departing from the four propositions and cutting off the hundred negations, one directly attains the state where the head of the storehouse is white and the head of the sea is black.

To set aside this matter and hold it up from the level above, even the wise remain confused and the adept lacks half. Leading the way in accordance with the unseen, the essence and its exposition differ.
Grasping a single phrase that encloses heaven and covers earth, changing the North Star and shifting the constellations—at this very moment, do not take even a single step forward.
If you step back one pace, then moving forward becomes narrow and retreating backward becomes spacious. Being spacious is sufficient for there to be room. You need not seek elsewhere;
you must simply believe that your own mind is the Buddha. The Buddha is your own mind; your own mind is the Buddha-mind;
the Buddha-mind is your own mind. When your own mind manifests, it is profoundly still and eternally abiding—unchanging, unshifting, and without end.
Movement is without agitation; there is no going and no coming, no increase and no decrease. Therefore, it is called the Buddha of Suchness (*tathatā*).
That which Kāśyapa realized in the past was this very mind; that which the World-Honored One transmitted was this very mind.

Bodhidharma’s “direct pointing to the human mind so that one may see one's nature and become a Buddha,” and the Second Patriarch’s “severing his arm to pacify his mind”—what they pointed to was this mind, and what he pacified was also this mind.
Apart from this very mind, there is no other dharma to be sought. Now, in seeking the unsurpassed Great Way, one must first clarify one's own mind.
If one's own mind is clarified, there is no separate Buddha outside the mind, and no separate mind outside the Buddha. Mind and Buddha are of one suchness; do not grasp at what is good.
Do not abandon evil. Neither rely upon nor depend on the two paths of purity and defilement. Let the mind that neither grasps nor rejects be present in every thought-moment.
Therefore, the three realms are nothing but mind; the myriad dharmas are nothing but consciousness. As the ancients said:

"Whatever forms one perceives are all perceptions of the mind. The mind is not of itself; it exists because of form. You need only speak in accordance with the occasion, such that phenomena and principle are one and the same.
There is nothing whatsoever that obstructs it. The fruit of the path to Bodhi is likewise: that which arises within the mind is immediately termed "form" (rūpa).
Because one knows form to be empty, arising is itself non-arising. If one understands this meaning, then one may dress and eat at the appropriate times.
By the waterside and beneath the forest trees, he nurtures the sacred embryo. When spring arrives, birds perch upon the shadowless tree;
when the time comes, flowers bloom upon the sproutless branch. Having reached such a state, he spreads out his staff—bent three times and four times—and drags along his sack—fragmented and scattered.
Sometimes, at a fork in the road, he builds a thatched hut and cooks pine flour to welcome those who come.
Come! Whether you go to the crossroads and cast yourself down entirely, blending with the mud and water to manifest transformation according to the species;

or whether you go to the summit of a solitary peak, clearing stones and chopping brush, using trees as beams to dwell together with wind and moon, and roam with monkeys and apes—what limit can there be to such joy?
Seizing a single phrase and deploying a single function, in every atom and every world, the wind of the original ground is fully revealed.

Light! In every dharma and at every turn, one must immediately sever the functioning of both extremes. At the very end, one transcends and liberates oneself spontaneously—like water returning to water, like space merging with space.
Since there are no traces left to be sought, how could there be any sound or form that does not penetrate?
If Jiaochong were to pour a second ladle of foul water over all of you, your feet would be shrouded in a vast expanse of blackness. Suddenly—
[The Master] picks up his whisk, draws a line, and says: "If you can discern the pivot here, it will illuminate the earth and shine upon heaven;
it will shatter the skull-caps of Buddhas and patriarchs and twist their nostrils around. Lofty and vast, it is utterly beyond this and that. You people of all [ranks], listen!"
"Is there still any effort to be applied here? After a long silence, he said: "Cease, cease! There is no need to speak. My Dharma is subtle and difficult to conceive. He addressed the assembly:
"When the World-Honored One ascended the seat, it was like a bountiful harvest; when Mañjuśrī struck the gavel, it was like a pampered child in a wealthy family. At that time...
A million beings among gods and humans—suppose someone had come forth and said, "Regarding today's affair, do not act so hastily.
Even if Mañjuśrī held a golden mallet in his hand, he would have had no place to strike it. It is a pity that no one uttered this turning word.
Had such a word been spoken, Mañjuśrī would be unable to turn back even to this day. Nevertheless, were it not for the early blossoming of flowers along the purple road...
Suddenly seeing a yellow oriole alight on a willow branch.
To the assembly: Within Tiantai Mountain, at Fangguang Temple, five hundred arhats are always present upon the Stone Beam Bridge.
"Seizing the wind and grasping shadows. Hanshan and Shide ride backward upon a fierce tiger and silently walk out.
At the mouth of the hemp bag and the tip of the staff, they limp and hobble, each dispersing on their own way. Everyone, tell me: after they have dispersed, what then?
After a long silence, he said, "Return to the hall for tea."
Addressing the assembly: The cypress tree in front of the hall is half-yellow and half-white; the seven-pound robe from Qingzhou is missing its eastern and western seams.
The founding patriarch feared being deceived by others; sitting upon the *pāṇḍu* stone, with every call and every nod, he could ultimately not escape it.
How is this to be seen? The cuckoo’s cry falls as the moon sinks at the third watch; butterflies flutter about above it.

Addressing the assembly: Lingyun attained enlightenment upon seeing peach blossoms, yet a conceptual understanding still remained. Xiangyan penetrated through upon hearing a bamboo strike, yet his intellectual ingenuity still lingered.
How can they compare to Wang Mahu of East Village, who neither knows nor understands, and uses whatever money he receives?
Addressing the assembly: Before Niu Tou had seen the Fourth Patriarch, the hundred birds brought flowers and the devas presented offerings.
Once the Fourth Patriarch saw him, the hundred birds no longer brought flowers and the devas no longer presented offerings. Tell me, where does the point of benefit and harm lie?
You must not resort to intellectual reasoning; try to offer a turning word. When the assembly’s words did not accord with the truth, the Master spoke on their behalf: "In the eye..."

"Not clinging to the sand. He addressed the assembly: "Standing atop the highest mountain peak, one does not understand how to descend from the sky; walking upon the deepest ocean floor, one does not understand how to surge forth from the earth.
What is the single phrase that overturns the box and its lid and cuts off all streams? The Master provided this substitute response: "O, the Great Void!"
He said, "The bright moon; the hall is empty. He also said, "The Stone Beam Bridge.

One day, the Master hung up the plaque for the private interview session for the assembly and gave this introductory remark: "When Nanquan cut off the cat, what was it like? The assembly offered various responses, none of which accorded with the truth.

At that moment, a servant standing nearby remarked, "The rat has grown too big. The Master laughed and said: (Note: This is a classic Zen koan regarding the story of Nanquan’s cat. The servant’s remark is intended as a non-conceptual, direct response that cuts through the duality of right and wrong.)
"What an excellent turning phrase! It simply should not have come from your mouth. Yuan asked for instruction.
The Master brought up the story of Zhaozhou’s examination of the old woman to interrogate him. Yuan said, "No one in the entire world can do anything with Zhaozhou.
The Master said, "I am not like that. Yuan asked, "How about you, Master? The Master said, "In the entire world..."
Diren could not withstand the old woman’s words. Yuan was enlightened by what she said.
[Later,] Wujian asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The Master opened his mouth and stuck out his tongue to show him. Wujian was at a loss for words.
The Master picked up his staff and drove him out. [Jian] went to see Master Zhen at Tianfeng; before he had even finished recounting the previous conversation, Zhen also struck him.
He returned to Xiamen Temple, where he had a realization while slipping on the muddy path. When he saw the Master, the Master said, "Why have you returned so quickly?
Jian said, "At that time, Master, you could not have struck me. The Master asked, "What did Tianfeng tell you?"

"Ma! I see you have recounted the circumstances of your journey. The Master struck him again. Although Jian had attained some realization, he ultimately could not bring himself to accept it as sufficient.
He subsequently built a hut on Mount Huading and exerted himself with rigorous asceticism. One day, while engaged in manual labor, his doubts were suddenly and completely resolved.
He rushed to Ruiyan to present his understanding. The Master certified him with a verse, saying: "The man of the Way has finally emerged from the mountains; he has fully laid bare his chest."
The chest opens toward me; it is vast and level like the surface of a mirror. It is clear and profound, utterly free from even a speck of dust. Suddenly, one finds the phrase for turning back:
with robes rolled up against the cold clouds, one simply returns home. At the Eighty-Thousand-Fathom Flower-Peak summit, a single laugh tears open the iron mask.
Once the home mountain is reached, all discursive thought ceases; one snaps the black staff and leans it against the bamboo gate.
The news from amidst the fire-pile of dung is good; when the aroma of taro is present, it is the very time of the Way’s fragrance.
He then entrusted him with the lineage and the dharma robe, speaking this verse: "This mind is utterly vast; even empty space cannot compare to it. This Way is exactly like this."
"Receive and uphold this; do not seek it elsewhere.
Regarding the "Inexhaustible Lamp," the Master held up his whisk and asked, "What is this? The Lamp also asked, "What is this? The Master said:
"Set aside the four great elements for me and speak another word. When the lamp moved from east to west, the Master lowered his left foot;
when the lamp moved from west to east, the Master lowered his right foot; when the lamp approached him, he stood with hands joined in *añjali*. The Master took up his whisk and struck him.
Deng paid his respects. On another day he asked, "When Bodhidharma came from the West, what exactly did he transmit?
The Master said, "Tell me, what has a person of this eastern land ever lacked? Deng said, "If there was nothing lacking, why did Shen Guang stand in the snow and cut off his arm?
The Master said, "It was simply to break up the family and scatter the property. At these words, Deng attained great enlightenment.
A monk asked, "The waters of Caoxi flow stream after stream toward the east; why does the water at Ruiyan flow toward the west?

The Master said, "You, Senior, do not recognize good from evil. The monk said, "I have come here specifically to ask about the water; why do you say I do not recognize good from evil? The Master said, "Blind fellow!"
As expected, he did not recognize [the master].
[The master] struck him. The monk asked, "What is the Buddha? The master said, "A patrolman violating the night curfew.
A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The master said, "Right now you have scratched me right where it itches."
A monk asked, "What is the essence of prajñā? The Master said, "An eight-cornered millstone. The monk asked, "What is the function of prajñā?
The Master said, "An eight-cornered millstone rolling through empty space."
A monk asked, "What is the essence of prajñā? The Master struck him. He asked again, "What is the function of prajñā? The Master struck him once more.
The Master once established three questions to test his students, saying: "Those who are truly outstanding and of superior caliber are like fine horses that, upon seeing..."
They move at the mere shadow of the whip. How could those of middling or inferior capacity hope to attain this?
To any eminent "cloud-and-water" practitioner whose words are precisely appropriate, I hand over the broken courtyard with both hands. He asked:
Why does one who steers an iron boat across the bottom of the sea cry out in distress within the eye of a needle?
Since he is the Great Master Linji, why must he undergo the plowing of the tongue-pulling ox?
Not established on that side, not proceeding to this side—cutting off the middle. Why does it not abide?
*The Recorded Sayings of Master Fangshan* (End) *Supplement*
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The Buddhas of the three periods and the six generations of patriarchs are beneath the feet of you all.

Is there anyone who can tread upon them? After a long silence, he said: "If you cannot tread upon them, then the Buddhas of the three periods and the six generations of patriarchs will defecate upon the crowns of your heads."
Ascending the hall, the mountain monk said: "All that I have spoken with you all during this summer retreat is nothing but talk of worldly convention;
it has no connection whatsoever with that matter. If you wish to accord with that matter, you must realize it directly within the midst of worldly convention.
If you do not do so, when you meet people in the future, you must by no means say that you spent the summer retreat at Jetavana."
Ascending the hall: One rooster, two dogs, three pigs, four sheep—the Buddha-dharma for the New Year has already been proclaimed.
Should you still linger in your observation and listening, you will see five horses, six oxen, seven people, and eight grains depart.

Ascending the hall, [the Master said: "When the hundred limbs have all decayed and scattered, there remains one thing that is eternally numinous. He took up his staff and said, "This here is the staff;
which one is that eternally numinous thing? He threw down the staff and said, "How does it compare to the tortoise-nosed snake of the South Mountain?"
Ascending the hall: For an entire summer, I have struck east and west, exhausted my hands and feet for your sakes until you were utterly worn out.
Fortunately, you remained serene and indifferent. Had even one or half a person allowed their eyes to flicker, I, the old monk, would certainly have fallen into the Avīci Hell.
Ascending the hall on the eighth day of the twelfth month: Seven in the Northern Dipper, eight in the Southern Dipper; night after night the light arises, and everyone’s eyes are alive.
Old Gautama suddenly exclaimed, "How marvelous! Is this planting trees? Planting bamboo? Planting fish? Planting vegetables?
Ascending the hall, he said: "The Zen practitioner’s bearing is like that of a king; how could he ever deign to lower his head to another?
Why has it come to this day, with everyone not daring to move so much as a single leaf on the ground? After a long silence, he said: 'Ninety days in the mountains.'"
"A thousand years beyond the clouds" (from the *Zengji xu denglu*, fascicle five; the biography of Chan Master Fangshan Bao of Jingci).
